outcome: The construction of a conservative, ergodic, sigma-finite (infinite) measure-preserving transformation with simple Lebesgue spectrum -- an affirmative answer to Banach's Scottish Book problem in its classical (infinite-measure/non-singular) reading -- was published by el Houcein el Abdalaoui well before the frozen revision date, with the cleanest write-up (arXiv:2210.15480) submitted 2022-10-27 and last revised 2023-06-09. Nothing in the 26 Jan 2024 - present window resolves, partially resolves, or moves a bound on the problem as Wikipedia states it; several adjacent but distinct spectral-multiplicity results appeared in the window (Sept 2024, June 2024) and none of them touch simple Lebesgue spectrum for an ergodic system in the sense at issue.
summary: Wikipedia's bullet states the classical Scottish Book question attributed to Banach: 'is there an ergodic system with simple Lebesgue spectrum?' The literature on this exact question (traced through el Abdalaoui's papers, which are the only substantive body of work on it) shows a layered history: a 2015 paper (arXiv:1508.06439) began the flat-polynomial approach; a 2020 paper (arXiv:2007.03684) gave an affirmative answer for the flow (R-action) version using rank-one flows; and a 2022 paper (arXiv:2210.15480, last revised 2023-06-09) gave a simplified, self-contained construction of a conservative ergodic sigma-finite measure-preserving transformation with simple Lebesgue spectrum, described by the author as answering Banach's Scottish Book problem affirmatively. All of this predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision by at least seven months, so under section 6.1 it is 'open_stale': settled (in this specific sense) before the window, never a change within it. Crucially, the resolved case is for a conservative, sigma-finite (i.e. generally infinite) measure-preserving transformation -- a non-singular dynamical system. The closely related but distinct question that Rokhlin posed, and that much of the survey literature treats as the 'basic' open problem -- whether a finite (probability) measure-preserving ergodic transformation can have simple Lebesgue spectrum -- is explicitly still reported as open in sources discussing this area (search results state 'the question of Rokhlin still remains open since the maps constructed does not have a pure Lebesgue spectrum' in the finite-measure setting). Wikipedia's own wording does not specify finite versus infinite measure, so which reading the bullet points to is ambiguous, but under either reading nothing changed within the window: if the bullet means the infinite-measure/Scottish-Book question, it was already resolved pre-2024 (open_stale); if it means the finite-measure/Rokhlin question, it remains open with no progress found in the window either. I searched specifically for 2024-2026 activity and found three adjacent papers -- 'Inducing countable Lebesgue spectrum' (Abdedou-Fayad-Thouvenot, arXiv:2409.00396, submitted 2024-08-31, showing every ergodic system induces a system with pure Lebesgue spectrum of *infinite* multiplicity, not simple/multiplicity-one spectrum), Ryzhikov's May/June 2024 paper on tensor powers and simple-versus-Lebesgue spectrum transitions under tensoring (arXiv:2406.08409), and a September 2026 paper on orbit equivalence of rank-one systems -- none of which settle, restrict, or move a bound on the simple-Lebesgue-spectrum question itself; they are related problems (different multiplicity, different operation) under section 3.1's scope rule, not cases of this problem. No AI system appears anywhere in any of the papers found; all are single- or multi-author pure-mathematics preprints from established ergodic theorists with no stated computational or AI assistance in either the mathematics or its exposition.
competing_reading: One could argue the bullet, being unqualified, should be read as already-resolved (open_stale) purely on the strength of the pre-2024 sigma-finite construction, full stop -- treating the finite-measure Rokhlin question as a separate Wikipedia entry's concern rather than this one's. Under that reading the classification is the same (open_stale) but the summary's caveat about the finite-measure case being separately open would be irrelevant noise. Conversely, one could argue the 'true' Banach/Scottish-Book question, as classically transmitted through Ulam's book and Rokhlin, was always implicitly about probability-space (finite-measure) transformations, in which case the sigma-finite construction is itself a 'related problem' rather than a resolution, and the correct status would be plain 'open' (never resolved even before the window) rather than 'open_stale'. I did not find a source that definitively fixes which reading Wikipedia intended, since the bullet cites only a single footnote reference without further qualification.
what_would_settle_it: The specific footnote/reference Wikipedia's bullet cites (footnote 37 in the frozen revision) would show which source the encyclopedia editors relied on and hence which version of the problem (finite- or infinite-measure) they meant. Locating and reading that exact citation would resolve whether 'open_stale' or plain 'open' (pre-existing, never resolved) is the more faithful classification; either way, no event in the 26 Jan 2024-present window is affected.
